intro: A quality is something every part of the engine must have so that a promise holds everywhere, not in one place. Each target below tells a situation at a show, in rehearsal, at the desk or in development, so that it can be tested: what happens, then what must be true. The targets say what is needed, never how to build it; where a number would make a target testable and no source gives one, the owner sets it.

targets.title: A power cut loses nothing of the game
targets.quality: Staying up through a live show
targets.situation: Mid-show, with two tablets connected and a video queued, the show machine loses power and comes back. When the engine runs again, the game is the same game: the same teams, scores, claimed tokens and exposed evidence, and the same answer to whether the game is in setup, running, paused or ended. Every tablet reconnects by itself under its own station name and shows the same facts as before. No scan made during the outage is lost or counted twice. The TV returns to the picture the game calls for, and a once-only cue that already fired does not fire again.
targets.numberToSet: how long the engine may take from power back to a running show
promises: Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
One game, the same on every screen
Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
targets.status: settled by the owner (the promise's need: a restart during a show loses nothing; the roadmap's aim that power on leads straight to a running show)
targets.why: A show that cannot survive a power cut or a crash needs a technician in the room every night, and the platform is meant to run without one.

targets.title: Crashed programs restart on their own
targets.quality: Staying up through a live show
targets.situation: During play the music player stops dead. The engine's program watcher restarts it a bounded number of times. While it is down the GM's panel says stopped, with no track; the controls come back within ten seconds with no reload. If the restarts run out, one red row with a Restart button appears. Cues that depend on music are held and shown as held, never silently dropped. The same holds for the video player, the sound system, the lighting system and the TV's browser.
targets.numberToSet: how many restarts the watcher tries, and over how long, before it shows red; confirm: ten seconds for the controls to come back (from the promise's test)
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's hardening block, its program watcher and self-heal; the glossary's entries on the program watcher, self-heal and held items; the promise's test)
targets.why: Outside programs crash; a show platform that others run must come back on its own and tell the GM only what it could not fix.

targets.title: A tablet reconnects to the same facts
targets.quality: Staying up through a live show
targets.situation: A tablet's wifi drops for a minute mid-show and comes back without a reload. During the minute every live panel shows that its numbers are old and the header says disconnected. For a scan the GM makes during the minute, the GM can always see what became of it: refused with a reason, or kept and answered when the connection returns. Which of the two a disconnected tablet does is not decided here; it belongs to the design round on where authority lives across devices, offline included. On reconnect the tablet is back under its own station name within five seconds and shows the same facts as a tablet that never dropped: a delete made meanwhile has freed its token, a reset has emptied the screen.
targets.numberToSet: confirm: five seconds for a tablet to be back under its own station name (from the promise's test)
promises: One game, the same on every screen
Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
targets.status: proposed (the promises' tests, which the owner has not ruled on one by one; the pass's question on how copies update and whether a screen shows their age). Open: what a disconnected tablet does with a scan, for the design round on where authority lives across devices, offline included.
targets.why: Venue wifi is weak and tablets roam; a reconnect that shows different facts is the kind of silent error that costs a GM's trust for good.

targets.title: Each scan counts exactly once
targets.quality: Staying up through a live show
targets.situation: A hardware scanner sends a batch of player scans. The engine restarts, and the scanner sends the same batch again. Each scan appears in the game exactly once. On another night a batch arrives while no game exists: the engine refuses it and the scanner keeps the scans, or the engine stores them. It never answers 'processed' while keeping nothing. Two presses of Skip in quick succession, where the second must fail, get one success and one failure, each matched to its own press.
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
targets.status: settled by the owner (the promise's goal and tests; the standing scanner decisions on final refusals and replayed scans in the project's guides for developers)
targets.why: Lost or doubled scans corrupt the night's record, and the record is what the director tells the players from.

targets.title: Screens say when the engine goes silent
targets.situation: The engine is killed while the TV shows the game clock and three player scanners sit ready. Within one check-in period (how often a scanner checks on the engine) each player scanner shows offline, and the TV shows its clock as unconfirmed and stops counting on its own. On every tablet each live panel says its numbers are old and how old. No screen anywhere shows a calm, current-looking value for a fact it cannot confirm.
targets.numberToSet: how long after the engine goes silent a screen must say so (today, how often the scanners check on the engine)
promises: Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
One game, the same on every screen
targets.status: proposed (the promise's goal: every fact and reply carries how old and how sure; the pass's question on how copies update and whether a screen shows their age; the promise's tests). The promises' tests are not yet ruled on one by one.
targets.why: A screen that looks right while it is wrong is worse than a blank one, because people act on it.

targets.title: Red means broken, grey means not installed tonight
targets.situation: The engine starts with a mistyped profile path. The tablet shows a red 'profile failed to load' row, the check before a game starts refuses, and no screen shows a calm green summary that reads as 'nothing installed'. On another night the profile says no lights are installed. Every lighting row and tile is grey, nothing is red, the lighting program is never started or restarted, and a cue with a lighting step finishes with a message that names the skipped step. Red appears only when something that should work does not.
promises: Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entries on not installed tonight versus a fault, and on the rule that red is shown only for a real fault, ratified 2026-09-04; the preflight entry's refusal on a broken profile, ruled 2026-09-12; the promise's tests)
targets.why: Red that is always red trains GMs to ignore red; the one night something really breaks, the red light must still be believed.

targets.title: A refused scan never reads as complete
targets.situation: The GM scans a token the engine will refuse: it was already claimed on another tablet, or the game is paused. The result screen never says 'complete'. It shows the engine's reason. The tablet shows no verdict of its own before the engine's arrives. In a standalone game the tablet is the decider, and the same holds: a scan into a paused game shows refused and records nothing.
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
One game, the same on every screen
targets.status: settled by the owner for the standalone case (the owner's decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed"); the rest is proposed (the promises' tests, which the owner has not ruled on one by one; the pass's question on who decides each fact)
targets.why: A device that judges for itself will one day disagree with the engine, and the GM will have told a team something untrue.

targets.title: The preflight states its own limits
targets.situation: The venue technician runs the preflight at home on a laptop with a simulation profile, then again at the venue with the real kit. Every line says whether it was checked on paper or live and against which profile. The home run never reads as a venue go. The lines the machine cannot check (the TV on the right input, tokens on set, a real tap firing a real video) appear as a short human checklist, never as green. The badge the designer sees in the editor uses the same words as the preflight at the show.
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's hardening block: the owner's ruling that the preflight states its own limits; the glossary's preflight and paper versus live entries; the rule that every screen quotes one verdict, ratified 2026-09-04)
targets.why: A go that overstates what was checked is the most expensive lie a tool can tell, because it is believed on opening night.

targets.title: A published change plays within minutes
targets.situation: On the show machine between games, the designer changes one token's rating in the design tool and publishes it. Within a set time, scoring, the token lists, the TV and every tablet use the new value, with no restart of the engine or any device; or the engine answers that it will apply the change at the next window between games; or it refuses and says why. The designer then plays a trial round and sees the new value awarded. A change can never reach a game that is running or paused.
targets.numberToSet: the minutes from publish to playing, the promise's 'within minutes'
promises: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's design-iteration loop; the promise's need and test; the owner's ratification of the design tool's pages, that applying a change refuses a running or paused game)
targets.why: Making games playtestable without code is the point of the engine work; a restart per change makes designers stop iterating.

targets.title: A broken pack is refused at the desk
targets.situation: The designer publishes a pack whose tokens name a group the pack never declares, and later one that needs an ability this engine does not have. Both are refused at the desk before anything reaches a running engine. Each message says which kind of refusal it is (the pack contradicts itself, or this engine cannot drive it yet) and names what is at fault. The live engine keeps the pack it has. Publishing an unchanged draft changes nothing.
promises: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entry on the check that refuses a broken pack, with its two refusal kinds; the glossary's draft and publish entry; the rule that every screen quotes one verdict, so mistakes are caught at the desk)
targets.why: A mistake caught at the desk costs a minute; the same mistake found by the GM on show night costs the show.

targets.title: A trial copy never touches the live show
targets.situation: While a show runs, the designer starts a separate trial copy of the engine on the same machine with a draft pack. The show's video player, music player, TV browser and sound watcher are untouched; the trial copy writes nothing into the show's records and issues no pass the show accepts. On a laptop with no hardware the trial copy reads every piece of equipment as not installed tonight and still plays the draft from start to end.
promises: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's preview block; the owner's ratification of the design tool's pages, that the trial copy ships with its own profile; the promise's test; the pass's question on whether anything but the live engine can touch the live show)
targets.why: Rehearsal that can hurt the live show is rehearsal nobody dares to do.

targets.title: A designer builds a whole game without code
targets.situation: A designer builds the toy game, or a new game of their own that uses only what the engine can already do, in the design tool alone: tokens and their content, modes, scoring, groups, cues, the clock, what each screen says. They open no code file and no configuration file. A mechanic they change reaches the hardware scanner as pack data; no device is re-flashed. The whole game runs on the engine with no engine change. A game that needs something the engine cannot yet do is refused at the desk with the missing ability named; that case has its own target under Easy to extend.
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome, the designer; the roadmap's platform parity rule: everything a designer iterates on is pack data, never firmware)
targets.why: Designers who are not technical are the platform's audience; the day a change needs a developer, the loop is closed to them.

targets.title: Set up the kit from the guide alone
targets.situation: A venue technician who has never seen the code receives the kit and the deployment guide. They build the show machine from the guide alone, fill in the profile for tonight's venue, bind each of the pack's names (lights, speakers, screens) to a real instrument on one page, and run the preflight. They get one go or no-go, and every line points to the setting behind it. Filling in the profile, binding the names and running the preflight happen in the tool's pages, with no terminal. Every gap they find in the guide is treated as a defect.
targets.numberToSet: how long the technician may need from an unpacked kit to a go
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's final outcome, the venue technician; the roadmap's readiness state adoptable; the roadmap's hardware testing and machine-swap method, gaps in the docs are doc defects); that building the machine itself needs no terminal is proposed (the clean-machine test in the promises includes an install line today)
targets.why: An open-source platform is taken up by strangers who stand it up from the guide, and the guide is proven only by someone who needs it.

targets.title: Power on straight into a running show
targets.situation: The GM plugs in the show machine and the TV. The machine powers on straight into a running show: the engine, the TV's resting picture, the video and music players, the kit network's name. Nobody opens a terminal or starts a program by hand. If something cannot start, the GM's tablet says what, in plain words, with the button to press.
targets.numberToSet: how long from power on to a running show
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's boot pain and the owner's ruling that the machine powers on straight into a running show)
targets.why: The owner's ask was 'a bit more plug and play'; a show that needs a technician to boot cannot be handed to anyone else.

targets.title: Every red row carries its own actions
targets.situation: Mid-show the Bluetooth speaker drops. The GM sees a red row that names the speaker and carries its actions: reconnect, re-route to the HDMI output, run without it. The GM picks one and the show goes on; if they choose to run without it, the row turns grey for the rest of the night and its cues skip that step quietly. The GM never needs a shell, a log file or a call to the developer during a show.
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's rule that every status row carries its actions; the glossary's entry on not installed tonight, and on the GM taking a service out of service for the night, ratified 2026-09-04)
targets.why: Status without actions is a dashboard; the GM's tablet is a control panel, and the GM is the only technician in the room.

targets.title: The engine writes the night's record by itself
targets.situation: The game ends. The engine writes the record of the night by itself: what was sold and exposed, by whom and when, the roster, the notes, the accusation and the photos captured during play, the pack and version the game ran, and the texts the players saw. Every time in it comes from one clock. The director's console, a separate program, reads that record directly; nobody pastes a report or re-parses a markdown file. The tablet's own downloadable report reads the same record, and its totals agree.
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
targets.status: settled by the owner (the owner's decision "The night's record and the after-game article": the record carries the pack and the texts the players saw, the console stays a separate program that reads the record, and the two clocks join the flaw "Tablets and phones decide facts the engine owns" as a finding; the roadmap's final outcome, the post-game report builds itself; the roadmap's capture block; the glossary's Review entry)
targets.why: The record of the night is what the director and the players are told from, and a platform others run must write it by itself, with one clock, so that nobody reconstructs a night from pasted text or corrects times by hand. Today the console has to shift the times back in two recorded games.

targets.title: Every fact is decided in one place
targets.quality: Easy to understand and change, for people and for AI agents
targets.situation: A developer or an AI agent is asked, for any fact a screen shows (is a video playing, which teams exist, may this token be scanned, which pack is running, is the lighting system up), where it is decided. They can name exactly one place, and every screen, reply and record that carries the fact traces to it. For every fact, the catch-up a reconnecting screen receives and the live message carry the same fields and values, and a test proves it. After engine start, after Reset System and after a test's reset, the engine is in the same state, and a test proves it. A test asks each question in two places at once and always gets one answer.
promises: One game, the same on every screen
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
targets.status: proposed (the pass's questions on who decides each fact, whether one question gets one answer, whether the catch-up after a reconnect matches the live message, and what each fact does between games; the glossary's words for the game's live facts, which name the facts and decide nothing about how the engine holds them; the promises' tests).
targets.why: An engine that others maintain and extend must let any reader find where a fact is decided and trust that every copy of it agrees; every extra answerer or second list of steps is a place a future change must find and will miss. At a show today, 'is a video playing' has eight answers, and start and reset follow two hand-kept lists.

targets.title: Every message and file is defined once
targets.quality: Easy to understand and change, for people and for AI agents
targets.situation: Everything that crosses the engine's edge (what a device may ask, what the engine answers, what it tells screens, and the files that carry a game or a night: the pack, the venue profile, the night's record, the media list) is written once in the published protocol, one versioned definition of every message and file the engine shares. Every program is generated from it or checked against it. A developer changes a field on one side only: a test fails and names the other side. A new message not in the definition cannot be sent or received.
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner (the owner's decision "One published protocol and an outside test bench"; the project's guide for developers and its rule that the written list of messages between the engine and the devices changes first; the promise's need: shared formats are written once)
targets.why: Names kept by hand on two sides drift silently; a single published list is what lets a stranger, or an agent, add a device without reading the engine.

targets.title: A newcomer proves a first change alone
targets.quality: Easy to understand and change, for people and for AI agents
targets.situation: A newcomer, a person or an AI agent, opens the repository cold. In one sitting they find: the glossary, the ten promises, the published protocol, and for each piece of the engine a short page that says what it decides, which promises it keeps and how it is tested. Every page matches the code; when work finds a disagreement, the same work fixes the page. The newcomer makes a small change and proves it on the test bench within a set time, without asking anyone.
targets.numberToSet: how long a newcomer may need to make and prove a first small change
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner for keeping documents true (the owner's decision "No rule for documents: fix as we go"; the process rules' writing standard; the roadmap's documentation system); the page per piece of the engine and the newcomer measure are proposed
targets.why: The owner's goal is an engine that is intuitive and easy to maintain and extend, and most of the people who will touch it, human and agent, have not seen it yet.

targets.title: No word of ALN's inside the engine
targets.quality: Easy to understand and change, for people and for AI agents
targets.situation: Search the engine's code for ALN's words: Black Market, Detective, memory, Account, any token id, any lighting scene name, any venue instrument. None appears outside ALN's pack and profile. The engine reads a mode's flags, never its name, and a pack's own word for a score-holder is what every screen shows. The toy game runs without any of ALN's words existing.
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rule that the engine holds no opinion; the glossary's section on ALN vocabulary as pack content; the promise's roles)
targets.why: Every ALN word in the engine is a place the second game breaks, and a place a new reader must learn one game to understand the platform.

targets.title: New abilities for a second game break nothing
targets.situation: A second designer builds a game with a scoring model, hidden per-player facts and multi-tap player actions that ALN never had. The game runs on the engine unchanged wherever the pack can declare what it needs. Where it needs an ability the engine lacks, the check refuses the pack and names the ability. Adding that ability is an additive change: ALN's pack and the toy game's pack run as before, every existing test passes, and the engine's version marks the addition.
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's second game's modules block, each module taking its parameters from the pack; the roadmap's players' phones block, multi-tap actions for both platforms; the glossary's entry on the abilities a pack requires (its Capability entry): ids are only ever added, never removed, and the pack lists what it needs)
targets.why: The business is one kit and many games; a game that needs an engine fork is not a pack.

targets.title: A new device kind joins by its pass
targets.situation: Someone brings a new kind of device: a different hardware scanner, a phone, a badge reader, a second scoreboard screen. It joins through the published protocol, presenting a pass that states its kind and role; a screen gets a read-only display pass. The engine learns the kind from the pass, never from the device's own word or the address it connected on, and gives it exactly what that role may see. For a remote display, the preflight counts the connected screens against the number the profile declares; for phones, the same once their number is set. The pack says which device classes its players use and what part each plays, and the phone's scanner and the hardware scanner drive the same pack-declared actions. A game that declares a new kind of display in its pack, such as the second game's constellation, can add the way it is drawn without changing the existing displays or any other game.
promises: Each person sees their part and can do only their part
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
One game, the same on every screen
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's platform parity rule; the hardening block's rulings that every connection presents a password or pass and the device's own type word is retired, 2026-09-12; the glossary's entries on remote displays and the watch-only pass, ruled 2026-09-12); a general way to add new kinds of display is room left beyond the constellation screen, with no slot yet (the roadmap's second game's modules block and the roadmap's row for deferred work on new kinds of screen defined by the pack)
targets.why: Devices and screens are the part of a kit that multiplies fastest, and a platform others run will meet kinds nobody planned; each new one must cost a pass and a count, never an engine change. Today a connection's own word decides what it gets.

targets.title: Replacing an outside program leaves the rest untouched
targets.situation: The venue swaps its lighting system, or a new video player replaces the old one. Supporting the new program changes nothing outside the code that talks to that program and the venue profile: no cue, pack, screen or test changes. Whether the engine starts the program itself or uses one already running is a plain setting, and the engine tells its own program from a stranger's copy of the same program. The same holds for programs that feed or read the engine: the designer replaces Notion with another authoring tool, which produces the same pack through the same check, and nothing downstream notices; after a game, ALN's director console, a separate program on another computer, reads the record of the night in its published format and needs nothing else from the engine.
promises: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
targets.status: settled by the owner (the promise's goal; the hardening block's ruling that the engine starts a program or uses one already running, 2026-09-12; the glossary's program watcher entry: how a program restarts is a setting on the show machine; the pass's question on how the engine reads the programs it runs; the roadmap's content tooling block, Notion as one replaceable source; the owner's decision "The night's record and the after-game article": the console stays a separate program reading the record, and the record is shaped so the console could later run inside Review)
targets.why: Venues and years change the programs around the engine; the engine should change in one place only, and what outside programs read and write must be published and stable.

targets.title: Nothing assumes one kit, one pack, one production
targets.situation: A second production buys a kit. They set it up with a new profile and the same engine code; no kit-specific name lives in the code, and the pack and the profile are chosen by name or id, never assumed to be the only ones. The engine is installed on a machine whose operating-system release has renamed the speaker rule and the TV's browser: it starts, logs no warning, and the TV page opens. Nothing in the engine assumes one kit, one pack or one production.
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rule on growth without corners; the promise's tests)
targets.why: A second kit is deliberately unplanned but must stay cheap to start; corners cut now are what make it expensive.

targets.title: A whole game runs with no venue hardware
targets.situation: On a laptop or a cloud machine with no venue hardware, a developer runs a whole game end to end: the engine, the GM tablet's app, both player scanners' software and the TV page, with stand-ins for video, sound, lights and speakers. Every lighting cue is checked against a stand-in light for each light the game names, generated from the pack's own needs. The same engine, the same pack and the same checks run at every test level (logic only; real programs with stand-in hardware; the home test bed; the venue), and each run records which checks it could not do and why. A designer rehearses the same way on a trial copy: every player action is available in a simulated form, framed as the player's act ('Team X scans the vault token'), and the show reacts for real. The simulation is an ordinary profile pointing at stand-ins; one can be generated from the pack's needs so that every need is met. The newcomer's first demo, the designer's try-my-change loop and the developer's test bench are one kind of rehearsal at different depths.
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entry on the test levels (the environment ladder) and its witness lights entry, ratified 2026-09-04 with every level as early as possible; the glossary's Rehearse and Simulation entries, ruled 2026-09-04; the owner's decision "Name each step by what it does", that test levels go by name; the promise's goal: tests run in levels)
targets.why: The show runs a few nights a month; everything that can only be proven at the venue is proven almost never, and a rehearsal that is a special mode drifts from the show.

targets.title: Every test runs twice and never skips silently
targets.situation: Every change to the engine runs the full set of tests twice, once with ALN's pack and once with the toy game's pack, and both must pass before the change reaches anyone. A test that cannot run on this machine fails loudly with its reason; a skipped, empty or silently passing test never counts as a pass. Every test stand-in for a real program or part is compared with the real thing it stands for: if a stand-in offers something the real program does not, or answers in a different format, the comparison fails and names the difference. The toy game stays in the repository for good.
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entries on the toy game's pack and on running the same test on two games, ALN and the toy game; the promise's need and tests on checked stand-ins and loud skips; the test-environment demand that tests skip loudly with reasons)
targets.why: One game proves nothing about being generic, a silent skip proves nothing at all, and a stand-in that drifts from the real thing makes every test above it a test of nothing.

targets.title: A test run cannot touch the live show
targets.situation: A live engine runs a show. On the same machine someone runs the whole test set. The show's music player, video watchers, sound watcher and TV browser all keep running, and the files that list the show's programs are unchanged. Every test run keeps its own files, network ports and settings, and cannot stop a program it did not start.
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
targets.status: proposed (the pass's question on whether anything but the live engine can touch the live show; the promise's test; the roadmap's rule on growth without corners covers kits and packs, not test runs)
targets.why: A test that can kill the show is a test nobody runs on show day, which is the day it matters.

targets.title: Players tap with no account and no login
targets.situation: A player walks in and taps a token on a shared station, or on their own phone. No account, no login, no app to install. The engine records a device or session id and nothing about the person. Nobody is named unless the game's design made an identification moment, and that moment is pack content, not an engine setting.
promises: Each person sees their part and can do only their part
Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rules on identity and player data, that players have no accounts and no login and that the only built-in identity is the device or session id; the roadmap's rule that the engine holds no opinion)
targets.why: These are the privacy defaults every future operator inherits; an engine that collects by default cannot give that back.

targets.title: Game data stays on the kit
targets.situation: After a game the roster, the notes, the photos, the scans and the record of the night are on the kit and nowhere else. They leave the kit only when the owner moves them (publishing an article, sending emails). How long each kind is kept is the owner's setting per game, and the engine keeps nothing past it. Players' email addresses stay outside the engine. The photo store is designed under these rules before the first photo is taken.
targets.numberToSet: the default retention per kind of data, per game
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
Each person sees their part and can do only their part
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rules on identity and player data, that game data stays on the kit and that retention is the owner's decision per game; the roadmap's capture block, its photo store under the privacy defaults; the owner's decision "The night's record and the after-game article", that players' emails stay outside the engine)
targets.why: Person-level data on a kit that strangers will one day run must have a home, a mover and an end date from the first design.

targets.title: Every request is checked against its pass
targets.situation: A stranger on the venue wifi opens a connection with no password or pass, calls itself a scanner and asks for the game state. It gets nothing. A connection holding a read-only display pass asks to pause the game: refused. Only staff who log in, such as the GM, can start, pause, end or reset a game, run show control or change a score, and the engine records which tablet did it. Every action is checked against what its pass allows, however it arrives, and is refused unless allowed. Before the first outside designer sits down with the tool, the committed lighting token and admin password have been rotated and the repository carries no live secret in any file or in its history; from then on an automatic test run fails if a live secret is committed.
promises: Each person sees their part and can do only their part
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's entry on the staff-only limit (starting, pausing and ending the game, show control and score changes stay with staff who log in, such as the GM), owner-fixed 2026-07-09; the roadmap's rules on identity and player data; the hardening block's ruling that every connection presents a password or pass, 2026-09-12; the roadmap's readiness states, the owner's ruling that the committed secrets rotate before the first outside person touches the system; the promise's tests); the automatic secret check is proposed
targets.why: A platform released to the public will sit on wifi it does not control and be run by strangers; every request must be checked, and the first outsider must not hold the owner's passwords.

targets.title: The engine filters before it sends
targets.situation: The TV connects. It receives only the events its role needs, and the catch-up it gets holds exposed evidence and team totals, never the full transaction list or the whole token file. In a game with hidden facts, a player's hidden fact reaches only that player's device. The engine filters before it sends; no device filters for itself.
promises: Each person sees their part and can do only their part
One game, the same on every screen
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's players' phones block, the access rules ratified 2026-07-17: filtering on the engine's side per screen; the pass's question on whether each screen gets only what its role needs; the promise's test)
targets.why: A screen that filters for itself has already been told the secret; hidden-information games are impossible on that footing.

targets.title: Sized for a two-hour show with headroom
targets.quality: Running well on the show machine and the venue network at the size of a show
targets.situation: Tonight's kit is one show machine (a Raspberry Pi), two GM tablets, three hardware scanners, two scoreboard screens, HDMI sound and one Bluetooth speaker, on the kit's own network with no internet. A full two-hour game runs at this size with headroom, and the engine is sized for one two-hour show for a few dozen devices: a GM scan is answered within a set time, a video reports started within half a second, every live message reaches every tablet within a set time, and the machine's load, memory, disk and temperature stay within set limits for the whole show. The preflight checks the machine's disk, temperature, processes and ports and shows each as go or no-go.
targets.numberToSet: the target kit size within a few dozen devices (tablets, scanners, screens, speakers); the scan answer time; the message delivery time; the machine's load, memory, disk and temperature limits; confirm: half a second for a video to report started (from the promise's test)
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
targets.status: settled by the owner for tonight's kit (the owner's account of how the venue runs, 2026-09-12), for the scale of a few dozen devices (the owner's decision "What the architects' panel sees, and when") and for the preflight's checks of the show machine (the glossary's preflight entry); the sizes and limits are proposed, and so is a preflight that refuses a start over a load limit
targets.why: The show machine is small and the show is live; the engine must be sized to it on purpose, not found out on the night.

targets.title: Phone capacity is measured before the first phone
targets.quality: Running well on the show machine and the venue network at the size of a show
targets.situation: Before any player phone is admitted to a game, the kit's capacity for phones is measured: how many phones one show machine and the kit's wifi carry while every scan stays answered within the set time and every tablet stays current. The number is written down before the first phone is admitted. The profile declares it and the preflight counts connected phones against it, as it does for remote displays.
targets.numberToSet: the number of player phones one kit carries
promises: Each person sees their part and can do only their part
Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
targets.status: settled by the owner in direction (the roadmap's players' phones block: kit capacity work precedes phone load); that the profile declares the number and the preflight counts phones against it is proposed, modeled on remote displays; no source gives the number
targets.why: Phones are the first load the kit has never carried; a number guessed on the night is a show that stalls.

targets.title: A small pack with checked media files
targets.quality: Running well on the show machine and the venue network at the size of a show
targets.situation: A pack stays small, measured in kilobytes, and names each media file by a fingerprint of its contents. The media bundle carries the files, moves between machines and is checked against the pack's list: a missing or changed file is named before the show, not found by a black screen. A hardware scanner's first sync from a blank card finishes within a set time and shows its progress on its screen; later boots transfer only the files that changed.
targets.numberToSet: the longest acceptable first sync for a hardware scanner (today 5 to 15 minutes for 30 to 40 MB)
promises: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
The game fits the venue it is in tonight
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's media model; the glossary's pack entry; the project's guide for developers, its first-boot expectation for the hardware scanner)
targets.why: Media is the heaviest thing the kit carries; a pack that is light and a bundle that is checked are what let a game move between machines.

targets.title: The whole show runs with no internet
targets.quality: Running well on the show machine and the venue network at the size of a show
targets.situation: The venue has no internet, and the kit's router has been replaced with another consumer router. The show runs in full. The new router needed three settings. The show machine answers the engine's name on the kit network, every device finds it, and no screen or device needs the outside internet for anything, the TV's typefaces included.
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked
targets.status: settled by the owner (the glossary's kit network entry; the roadmap's visible-change list, the wall scoreboard's typefaces served from the kit)
targets.why: The kit brings its own network because venues cannot be trusted to; one hidden dependence on the internet is a blank TV at the venue.

targets.title: A standalone game is normal, never a fault
targets.situation: The game declares itself standalone. Each device, the GM tablet and every player scanner, starts with no engine and says 'standalone', not 'offline' or 'disconnected'. Nothing shows red for the missing engine; every service the engine runs (video, music, lights) reads grey, as not installed tonight. The tablet decides teams, claims, scores, evidence and whether the game is in setup, running, paused or ended under the same rules as the engine, and a test proves the two equal. The game can be named, paused and ended; a scan into a paused or ended game is refused with a reason and the token stays unused; starting the next game does not delete the finished one.
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says
One game, the same on every screen
targets.status: settled by the owner (the owner's decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed": a whole game run with no engine, as a choice a game can declare; the promises' tests; the glossary's entry on the rules the engine and a standalone tablet share); open: how many tablets one standalone game may have, and where the standalone fact is kept
targets.why: A game with no engine is a choice a game may declare, and a platform that will run in rooms with no network must treat that choice as normal, never as a fault. Today every device reads it as an outage all night.

targets.title: No game mixes engine and standalone devices
targets.situation: A game is declared standalone and a device tries to join it through an engine; or a game is networked and a device tries to play it alone. In both cases the mix is refused and the device says why. No game ever has some devices on an engine and some alone.
promises: The game fits the venue it is in tonight
One game, the same on every screen
targets.status: settled by the owner (the owner's decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed": no game mixes networked and standalone devices)
targets.why: A mixed game has two deciders and no way to reconcile them; refusing the mix is cheaper than every later fix.

targets.title: A standalone game leaves its own record
targets.situation: A standalone game ends. The tablet's record of the night carries the pack and the version it ran, and the GM can download the report. The hardware scanner plays a standalone game as the phone's scanner does: it shows the token's content, plays the sound and keeps its own list, and its missing standalone mode is closed as a parity gap, not added as a new feature, if you confirm that reading (your open question [[q:L]]).
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner in part (the owner's decision "Standalone games: declared, never mixed"; the pack promise's goal: the game's record carries the pack's version); open: the hardware scanner's reading, recorded as a parity gap on the owner's parity rule and still waiting for the owner's explicit word (the owner's open question "The hardware scanner's standalone mode"); whether a standalone game's record holds what the players found at all (the owner's open question "One GM tablet per standalone game?"), and how exposure and video tokens behave with no engine
targets.why: Standalone games are on the list every design must serve; a record that exists only in networked games makes them second-class.

targets.title: Offline scans are kept and sent once
targets.situation: In a networked game the network fails for a hardware scanner mid-show. It keeps each scan on its card, shows the player a result that says the scan is kept and not yet sent, and never promises a video it cannot start. When the network returns, the kept scans are sent once and appear in the game once. A live scan refused because no game exists is shown as refused and never kept for later (the standing scanner decision). Scans already kept, sent when no game exists, follow the batch rule: the device keeps them or the engine stores them, and the engine never answers 'processed' with nothing kept. The phone's scanner behaves the same way.
targets.numberToSet: how many scans a device must be able to keep while offline
promises: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards
Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question
targets.status: settled by the owner (the standing scanner decisions in the project's guides for developers: a final refusal is never queued, a replayed scan never triggers a video; the promise's test on a batch sent twice)
targets.why: Weak wifi is the normal case at a venue; a device that lies about what it kept makes the record and the player's trust both wrong.

targets.title: The machine matches what it should carry
targets.situation: The owner sends a new version to the venue. The show machine carries one written list of what it should hold: the engine's version, the tablet and phone apps, the pack, the media and the venue profile. A status check at start compares the machine with that list and names any piece that differs; a mismatch between an engine and a tablet shows on the GM's screen when the tablet connects. Rolling back moves every piece, and the check lists any that did not.
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner (the promise's need and test: the machine carries everything on one written list of what it should carry; the roadmap's operations era and release block, steady-state releases; the roadmap's method for swapping in the new machine)
targets.why: The owner can only send what the machine can prove it holds, and can only roll back what moves as one set; today nothing stops a machine quietly running a mixture of versions.

targets.title: Replugging the old machine undoes a release
targets.situation: Nothing reaches the show machine until the owner says the new engine is ready. After the swap, the engine changes only between events, while packs may be published at any time. If the new machine fails on a show night, the owner plugs the old machine back in; it takes the same network address and name, and every tablet, scanner and screen carries on without noticing the machine changed.
promises: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rule that nothing deploys to the live machine until the show-ready decision; the roadmap's method for swapping in the new machine (blue, the show machine in use now, and green, the new one); the roadmap's operations era and release block, engine updates only between events)
targets.why: A release the owner cannot undo in a minute is a release the owner will not make.

targets.title: Running copies of the engine stay separate
targets.quality: More than one copy, kit or pack without rework
targets.situation: Two running copies of the engine share one machine: the show's copy and a trial or test copy. Each keeps its own files, network ports and settings; neither can stop the other's programs, read its records or accept its passes. A kit holds a library of installed packs and the operator picks one per event. A second kit on another machine needs a profile and nothing else. None of this requires a change to engine code.
targets.numberToSet: how many copies of the engine one machine must carry at once
promises: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices
A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show
The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays
targets.status: settled by the owner (the roadmap's rule on growth without corners; the roadmap's operations era and release block, multi-game kits; the owner's decision "Design top-down, hardest-to-reverse choices first", whose list of design rounds names how one engine runs as many separate copies)
targets.why: The trial copy, the test run and the second kit all need the same thing, one copy that keeps to itself; built once, it serves all three.
